summary: Explains how to translate between the older Diversion header field and the standardized History-Info header field in SIP, both used to describe call forwarding. The Diversion header is non-standard but still widely deployed, so systems need a way to interwork.

eli5.summary: Two phone systems write down where a forwarded call came from in different notes. This document is the translation guide between the two note styles.

subtitle: A translation guide between the old Diversion header and the standard History-Info header for forwarded SIP calls.

tldr.problem: SIP call-forwarding details travel in two different header fields: the non-standard Diversion header, widely implemented, and the standard History-Info header. Networks using different ones cannot read each other's diversion information.
tldr.mechanism: An interworking function at the border maps each Diversion entry to a History-Info entry, and the reverse, translating reasons to cause codes, counters to indexes and privacy settings between the two. Both headers must not coexist unmanaged in one INVITE.
tldr.outcome: Operators can migrate from Diversion toward History-Info without losing who forwarded a call or why. RFC 7544 obsoletes RFC 6044, and new use of Diversion is strongly discouraged.

facts.label: Entries created
facts.value: N Diversion entries become N+1 History-Info entries

today: RFC 7544 is an Informational Independent Submission that obsoletes RFC 6044; the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it. It describes a migration aid, and says new use of the Diversion header is strongly discouraged.

sections.title: Two Headers for Call Diversion
sections.content:
Services such as voicemail, interactive voice response or automatic call distribution work better when the called SIP user agent knows who diverted the session and why. Two SIP header fields can carry this: History-Info from RFC 7044 and the historic Diversion header from RFC 5806.

Diversion is not standardized but is widely implemented, because the first SIP deployments used it when no standard solution was ready. History-Info is the IETF solution and is more general, since it records all retargeting, not only call diversion. The RFC says new implementation and deployment of Diversion are strongly discouraged. It obsoletes RFC 6044, which covered the same mapping against the older RFC 4244 version of History-Info.

The main structural difference is order. History-Info is chronological, with the oldest entry first. Diversion uses reverse chronology, so the first entry read is the last diverting user.
sections.eli5: Two phone companies keep notes about who passed a call along. One writes the newest note first, the other writes the oldest first. This guide explains how to copy notes from one style to the other.

sections.title: Scope and General Rules
sections.content:
The interworking is meant to be done by a SIP border device, an interworking function (IWF), that knows by configuration it sits between a History-Info region and a Diversion region. It applies to INVITE requests. In 3xx responses it should apply when a proxy wants to interwork with the other kind of network. History-Info in other SIP responses (except 100) is not used for call forwarding and should not be changed into Diversion.

Because both headers describe forwarding, they could contradict each other, so they must not independently coexist in the same signaling. When a Diversion network feeds a History-Info network, the Diversion header must be replaced and removed in the outgoing INVITE. When going the other way, a History-Info header holding only forwarding data must be deleted after mapping. If it holds other information, it must stay unmodified and be forwarded, because it also serves as a session history. If both headers arrive together, only the information missing from the target header is added as the most recent entry.

The recommendation is to use local policies that minimize loss of information. The RFC also notes that implementations which do not use the cause URI parameter for forwarding are not covered by the mapping.
sections.eli5: A translator stands at the border between two countries. Notes that are only about forwarding get rewritten and the old copy thrown away, but notes with extra information get passed along untouched.

sections.title: Privacy Handling
sections.content:
Forwarding data names real people, so privacy matters. A Privacy Service at a domain boundary anonymizes addresses by replacing them with anonymous@anonymous.invalid. For History-Info this is driven by a Privacy header with the value history (or header in the message). For Diversion it is driven by the privacy parameter, where full, uri or name triggers anonymization and the parameter is then removed.

When mapping, Diversion privacy=full, name or uri becomes history, and off becomes an absent or none Privacy header. In the other direction history becomes full and absent or none becomes off. The privacy mapping must only be considered within a trusted domain that ensures privacy requirements are applied correctly.
sections.eli5: If someone asked to keep their name secret, the translator must keep it secret in both note styles, and only inside a place where everyone follows the rules.

sections.title: Mapping Diversion to History-Info
sections.content:
For N Diversion entries, N+1 History-Info entries are created, mapping Diversion from the bottom-most entry to the top-most so the history reads in session order. An extra final entry holds the Request-URI of the received INVITE. Each entry after the first gets a cause URI parameter from the previous Diversion entry's reason, and an mp parameter pointing to the preceding entry's index. Indexes grow by appending .1.

When a Diversion counter is greater than 1, placeholder entries such as sip:unknown@unknown.invalid are created so the number of diversions is preserved. A tel URI that must carry extra parameters is converted to a SIP URI with user=phone and the domain unknown.invalid. Other Diversion parameters have no History-Info equivalent and get no recommendation.
sections.eli5: If a call was passed along three times, the translator writes four lines. The last line is who finally got the call, and each line points back to the one before it.

sections.title: Mapping History-Info to Diversion
sections.content:
One Diversion entry is created for each History-Info entry whose cause parameter has a value listed in RFC 4458. The entry with the cause is the Target_entry. The diverting party is found through its mp parameter, or in the preceding entry if mp is absent. History-Info is read top-most to bottom-most, so the first selected entry becomes the last Diversion entry.

The address becomes the Diversion name-addr, the cause becomes reason, and the counter is set to 1. Where several History-Info entries come from forking, the interworking entity may map only some, according to local policy. Section 7 of the RFC works examples end to end, including a call crossing two History-Info networks and one Diversion network. It also covers coexistence in a mixed network, where equivalence between the two headers must be maintained and a gap in History-Info is marked with a 0 index.
sections.eli5: Going the other way, the translator reads the old notes, finds each place the call was handed on, and writes a short line for each, newest first.

sections.title: Security and Compatibility
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7044 and RFC 5806 apply, along with the privacy rules above. Without integrity protection, requested privacy could be downgraded or removed. Without confidentiality, eavesdroppers could read personal information the user asked to hide. Unauthorized insertion, deletion or modification of these headers can mislead users and applications.

For backward compatibility, the RFC points to the evolution of History-Info from RFC 4244 to RFC 7044 and to the compatibility section of RFC 7044. Appendix A adds a similar mapping between Diversion and the Voicemail URI of RFC 4458, which carries one redirecting user and a reason in the Request-URI.
sections.eli5: If someone could secretly change the notes, they could fool the person getting the call, so the notes must be protected and kept private when asked.
